images.alt: An AT&T Teletype DMD 5620 terminal, a beige CRT unit with a small keyboard
images.caption: The 5620 line descends from the Blit, the bitmapped terminal Rob Pike and colleagues built at Bell Labs; Plan 9's windowing ideas trace back to programs written for machines like this one.
images.author: Marcin Wichary

images.alt: Three vintage computer terminals on display: a VT52, an ADM-3A, and an AT&T 5620
images.caption: The AT&T 5620 (right) alongside earlier character terminals shows the leap it represented: a real bitmap display and local CPU, able to run multiple windowed programs Unix mainframes could not.
images.author: Seth Morabito

images.alt: Aerial view of the AT&T Bell Laboratories complex at Murray Hill, New Jersey
images.caption: Bell Labs' Murray Hill, New Jersey campus is where Unix, C, and later Plan 9 were built by the Computing Sciences Research Center through the 1970s and 1980s.
images.author: United States Geological Survey (USGS)

images.alt: Brian Kernighan and Ken Thompson standing together at an event
images.caption: Ken Thompson (right), co-creator of Unix, was also a member of the Computing Sciences Research Center team that built Plan 9, the operating system 9front continues today.
images.author: A.C.Diller

images.alt: Dennis Ritchie at a 1984 USENIX conference gathering in the mountains near Salt Lake City
images.caption: Dennis Ritchie, co-creator of Unix and the C language, worked in the same Bell Labs research group that later produced Plan 9 and, from it, 9front.
images.author: Perry Kivolowitz

images.alt: Glenda, the rabbit mascot of Plan 9 from Bell Labs, a simple line-drawn white rabbit
images.caption: Glenda, drawn by Bell Labs researcher Renée French, has been Plan 9's mascot since the 1990s and still appears throughout 9front's tools and documentation.
images.author: Renée French
